Consider carefully: if you find it hard to sit for long periods repeatedly verifying documents and data, cannot tolerate strict declaration deadlines and the consequences of error, or are unwilling to explain matters to clients while holding the compliance line, the actual work will differ from your expectations.

The work of customs brokers can be divided into three connected but distinct work areas. The first is tariff classification and document preparation: classifying merchandise under the tariff coding system, preparing and processing import and export documents that comply with customs laws, obtaining and compiling customs invoices, certificates of origin and freight control documents, and reporting data to government agencies. The second is duty and tax handling: calculating and tracking the duties and taxes owed, quoting under the federal tariff schedule and excise taxes, paying amounts on behalf of clients, applying for duty concessions, refunds and rebates, and preparing duty protest materials for clients where there is a basis. The third is client and logistics coordination: explaining import and export restrictions, the tariff system, insurance requirements and quotas to importers and exporters; signing documents and arranging or assisting with guarantees on behalf of clients under a power of attorney; arranging transport, warehousing and distribution; contracting with freight forwarders, tracking cargo location and arranging insurance; keeping in contact with customs brokers at other ports and negotiating with officials of various agencies to expedite clearance. The three work areas alternate, but their basis, responsibility and risk differ; so do client types, systems and authorization scopes across settings such as customs brokerage, in-house corporate customs affairs and logistics services.

Where are the boundaries between customs brokers and adjacent purchasing management and transportation management positions?

This table compares customs brokers with the adjacent occupations of purchasing managers, transportation, storage and distribution managers, buyers and purchasing agents for farm products, and wholesale and retail buyers except farm products, across seven items — core purpose, main objects and basis, core process, main outputs, responsible party, collaboration and supervision, and boundary of conclusions: adjacent occupations all involve purchasing or the movement of goods, but the objects, whether the role is entrusted with customs clearance and authorized signing, and whether it carries purchasing decision or logistics management responsibility do not shift just because the occupations are adjacent; compare item by item against actual duties and the process you work in.
Core purpose

Compile and declare cargo information on behalf of importers and exporters, handle classification, documents and taxes, coordinate clearance and keep reviewable records; customs review, collection and release decisions belong to the competent authority and are not exercised by the broker.

Core purposes of adjacent occupations: purchasing managers plan and direct the purchasing activities and purchasing staff of an organization or department; transportation, storage and distribution managers plan and coordinate transportation, storage or distribution activities under policies and regulations; buyers and purchasing agents for farm products purchase farm products for processing or resale and assess quality and price; wholesale and retail buyers except farm products purchase merchandise for wholesale or retail and negotiate supply terms.
Main objects and basis

The import and export goods and documents entrusted by clients, tariff codes, duties and taxes, and transport and warehousing arrangements; the basis is customs laws and the tariff schedule, import and export restrictions and quota rules, the client's power of attorney and scope of engagement, and the employer's review and escalation paths.

Objects and basis of adjacent occupations: purchasing needs and suppliers (purchasing managers), transportation, storage and distribution networks and regulations (transportation, storage and distribution managers), farm products and quality standards (buyers and purchasing agents for farm products), merchandise and supply terms and market demand (wholesale and retail buyers).
Core process

Receive the engagement and verify authorization → review the goods and documents → propose a classification under the tariff schedule → prepare declaration materials → verify the taxes and application conditions → coordinate logistics and track the customs processing status.

Processes of adjacent occupations: formulate purchasing strategy and manage purchasing staff (purchasing managers), plan and coordinate transportation, storage and distribution resources (transportation, storage and distribution managers), inspect and evaluate and purchase farm products (buyers and purchasing agents for farm products), compare prices, negotiate and place merchandise orders (wholesale and retail buyers).
Main outputs
Classification bases, import and export documents, tax calculation and payment records, relief and refund applications, authorized signed documents and cargo tracking records.

Outputs of adjacent occupations: purchasing strategy and contracts (purchasing managers), logistics plans and operating records (transportation, storage and distribution managers), farm product purchase contracts and quality inspection records (buyers and purchasing agents for farm products), purchase orders and supply contracts (wholesale and retail buyers).
Responsible party

In the United States, brokers act under their license and scope of engagement and bear responsibility for supervising and controlling brokerage operations; in China, customs brokerage enterprises must reasonably review the authenticity of the entrusted materials, and liability for declaring in the name of the client or in their own name is verified separately. Employee duties are set by the division of authorization and review, and full responsibility cannot be placed solely on the individual handling the matter.

Responsible parties of adjacent occupations: purchasing managers are responsible for purchasing strategy and purchasing outcomes; transportation, storage and distribution managers for logistics operations and compliance; buyers and purchasing agents for farm products for the quality and price of the farm products purchased; wholesale and retail buyers for merchandise purchasing and supply terms.
Collaboration and supervision

Collaborate with clients, freight forwarders, fellow customs brokers and customs and other bodies within the scope of authority. Editorial check suggestion: when a regulation or fact needs verification, refer it to authorized personnel through valid procedures and keep records, and it must not be equated directly with a violation or excess of authority; unauthorized or unlawful actions must not be carried out. The specific conditions for pausing, continuing and resuming a declaration are verified against the applicable jurisdiction and the valid agency or employer procedures.

Collaboration of adjacent occupations: purchasing managers collaborate with internal departments and suppliers; transportation, storage and distribution managers collaborate with carriers and warehouse operators; buyers and purchasing agents for farm products collaborate with farmers, processors and quality inspection; wholesale and retail buyers collaborate with suppliers and sales departments.
Boundary of conclusions

Similar job titles do not mean the same duties: whether the focus is entrusted customs brokerage and import/export compliance, organizational purchasing management, transportation and warehousing and distribution management, farm product purchasing, or merchandise purchasing and supply — and whether the role carries authorized signing, tax payment on behalf of clients, or management responsibility — determines the scope of duties and how performance is assessed, and the roles cannot be swapped by title.

The preparation levels and authorization conditions of adjacent occupations do not apply to this occupation; verify them item by item against each occupation's official materials and the requirements of your employer.
Key occupational judgments

Six recurring professional judgments: whether merchandise classification and tariff application are accurate; whether import and export documents, certificates of origin and freight control documents are complete and consistent; whether the calculation, payment, relief and refund of duties and taxes comply with the rules; whether declaration and clearance are handled under the applicable jurisdiction, laws and procedures; whether client instructions and authorized signing fall within the power of attorney and scope of engagement; and whether, when regulations are uncertain, something exceeds your authority or a client requests non-compliance, you verify first, refuse and escalate.
Classify merchandise under the tariff coding system and state the basis; incorrect classification leads to tax errors and compliance risk.

Verify that import and export documents, customs invoices, certificates of origin and freight control documents are complete and consistent; missing or inconsistent items affect clearance and later verification.
Calculate and track taxes as required, pay on behalf of clients and handle relief and refunds; improper handling causes collection errors and client losses.
Declare under the applicable jurisdiction, laws and procedures and negotiate clearance with the various agencies; deviating from procedure makes the declaration invalid or gives rise to disputes.
Judgment four: Are declaration and clearance handled according to procedure?

Signing documents and arranging or assisting with guarantees under a power of attorney must fall within the client's authorization and scope of engagement; signing beyond authority brings legal liability.
Judgment five: Is the signing within the scope of authorization?

Editorial check suggestion: first distinguish between a regulation or fact that needs verification, something beyond your authority, and a client's non-compliant request, and verify the authorized reviewers and valid escalation procedures for each separately; do not carry out unauthorized or unlawful actions, and do not uniformly write all pending items as refusals or suspensions of filing.

Work context and working conditions

Customs brokers work mainly in an office, requiring long periods of sitting and continuous use of a computer and telephone, frequent communication with clients and agencies, and pacing the work according to declaration deadlines and brokerage volume;

U.S. O*NET work context: email and telephone 100% every day, 85% indoors in a controlled environment every day; 90% never exposed to outdoor weather, 95% never exposed to hazardous conditions. The percentages are respondents' opinions, not Chinese job locations or a safety guarantee; the on-site arrangements of brokerage firms, corporate customs affairs and logistics positions must be verified separately.

Main objects and equipment | The import and export goods and related documents entrusted by clients, tariff codes and rate materials, computers and brokerage business systems, tariff and classification tools, telephones and email; the O*NET technology profile lists technology keywords such as Microsoft Office, Microsoft Excel, Microsoft Outlook, Microsoft PowerPoint, Microsoft Word, SAP and Microsoft Access; the list of objects and tools comes from this occupation's tasks and technology profile and is not a purchasing or authorization recommendation.

Editorial process illustration: receive the engagement and verify authority, review the goods and documents, propose a classification and verify the applicable rules, prepare declaration materials, handle taxes and applications within authority, and track customs processing; hand over unfinished matters. The specific sequence depends on the merchandise, jurisdiction and unit process and does not replace a customs release decision or the statutory declaration deadline.

These do not describe Chinese shift arrangements or overtime pay, and arrival and declaration deadlines should be verified at interview.

Report to a supervisor or along the review path; work context responses listed on the current O*NET page for U.S. Customs Brokers (13-1041.08) (page marked as updated in 2026; the specific survey period was not obtained): 75% rated "continual contact with others" as the highest level, 60% rated collaboration with a team as extremely important and 30% as very important, 68% said there are face-to-face discussions every day, and 40% said they deal with unpleasant or angry people once a week or more but not every day.

U.S. O*NET respondent opinions: 80% consider accuracy extremely important and 15% very important; for the consequences of errors that are hard to correct, 25% say extremely serious, 30% serious and 30% fairly serious. General automation is 40% high and 40% moderate, not a GenAI adoption rate. values: Fictional customs brokerage scenario material (exercise input)

Fictional scenario: a customs broker encounters four problems while on duty. First, a shipment's declared classification looks suspicious and the client insists on declaring at a lower rate; second, one document is missing a certificate of origin and the client asks to declare first and supply it later; third, a client asks to sign a document on their behalf that is outside the scope of the power of attorney; fourth, a tax calculation forwarded by a coworker lacks the verification process and basis.

Materials provided: key points of tariff classification; document verification requirements; the scope of the power of attorney and the matters that can be handled; tax calculation and record standards.

Materials not provided: who holds decision authority in classification disputes, the time limits and consequences of supplying documents later, how to handle documents outside the authorization, and the division of responsibility for tax errors. If the exercise requires these conditions, state your assumptions and the people you need to confirm with.
Task requirements

Please write a one-page handling and reporting plan covering: verification and handling recommendations for a suspicious classification, how to handle a missing certificate of origin, how to respond to a request to sign beyond your authority, and completing and verifying the tax calculation record.
The plan must state which information comes from the given materials and which is still assumption, and indicate whether the basis is the tariff schedule, regulations or record standards.
Reference deliverable (can be derived from the prompt)

The plan should include: suspicious classification (verify merchandise attributes and the classification basis under the tariff schedule, explain to the client that declaration follows actual attributes and not a lower rate, and refer disputes to the authorized position for a decision), missing certificate of origin (explain the impact and the process for supplying it according to the document verification requirements, do not declare first and supply later on your own, and apply for an extension or report upward according to procedure when necessary), signing beyond your authority (explain the scope of the power of attorney, refuse to sign on their behalf and refer it to authorized personnel), incomplete tax records (complete the calculation basis and the verification process, and do not guess at missing content), and handover (state the status of the four items, the actions taken and the matters still to be confirmed).
The reference deliverable only lists the elements that should be included and does not require wording identical to the example; being able to explain the basis for your judgments is enough.
Boundaries and conclusions that cannot be inferred

This item only tests awareness of classification, document verification, authorization boundaries and compliance escalation; it does not evaluate whether the handling of any real case is compliant, and it does not constitute a compliance determination, liability determination or legal advice.

Do not use real client data or unredacted commercial information; where real customs declaration, taxes and client information protection are involved, the law, competent-authority rules and unit policies must be followed.

values: Day 1: Read a public document
Find a public educational document on customs declaration or the tariff schedule, mark three key requirements and the corresponding practices, and write down the points you want to confirm.

entries.answer: Prepare customs documents on behalf of importers and exporters and ensure goods comply with applicable law: classify merchandise under the tariff coding system; prepare and process import and export documents under customs laws; obtain and compile customs invoices, certificates of origin and freight control documents; calculate and track the duties and taxes owed, quote under the tariff schedule and excise taxes and pay amounts on behalf of clients; explain import and export restrictions, the tariff system, insurance requirements and quotas to clients; sign documents and arrange or assist with guarantees on behalf of clients under a power of attorney; apply for duty concessions, refunds and rebates and prepare protest materials; arrange transport, warehousing and distribution, track cargo location and arrange insurance; and report data to government agencies.
entries.question: What does the daily work of a customs broker involve?

entries.answer: This occupation handles customs declaration, tariff classification and import/export compliance on behalf of clients and carries authorized signing and payment of taxes on their behalf; purchasing managers center on organizational purchasing management and supplier strategy; transportation, storage and distribution managers center on logistics operations and management; buyers and purchasing agents for farm products center on farm product purchasing and quality inspection; wholesale and retail buyers (except farm products) center on merchandise purchasing and supply negotiation; cargo and freight agents center on transport arrangement and carrier coordination; compliance officers center on review and investigation of broader compliance matters. subject.name: Customs Brokers
subject.summary: In the United States, customs brokers correspond to O*NET-SOC 13-1041.08 (Customs Brokers), preparing customs documents on behalf of importers and exporters and ensuring goods comply with applicable law in order to facilitate import and export: classifying merchandise under the tariff schedule, preparing and processing import and export documents, obtaining and compiling customs invoices, certificates of origin and freight control documents; calculating and tracking the duties and taxes owed and paying amounts on behalf of clients; signing documents and arranging or assisting with guarantees on behalf of clients under a power of attorney; advising clients on import and export restrictions, the tariff system, insurance requirements and quotas; applying for duty concessions, refunds and rebates and, where there is a basis, preparing duty protest materials for clients; arranging transport, warehousing and distribution, contracting with freight forwarders, tracking cargo location and arranging insurance; reporting data to government agencies and keeping in contact with customs brokers at other ports to expedite clearance. The preparation level for this occupation is Job Zone Three (SVP 6.0 to below 7.0); on O*NET its wage, employment and industry data are published under the parent occupation "Compliance Officers" (13-1041.00), not values collected separately for this subcategory. Comparable positions in China are customs declaration, customs affairs and import/export documentation positions in customs brokerage enterprises and declaring units; their duties and authorization basis do not correspond one-to-one with this U.S. occupational subcategory and cannot be interchanged.
